narrative:
The model estimates a 48% chance that you will leave your job, which is high enough for the company to deny your promotion as a precaution.

Three factors stood out in the decision. First, your total years of professional experience had the strongest influence, and it pushed the prediction toward you staying. Most employees the model expects to remain have similar short-to-mid experience levels, so this worked in your favor. However, two other factors pulled more strongly in the opposite direction. The fact that you have received other job offers while working here was the second most important signal and increased the likelihood of leaving. Finally, the relatively short time you have spent in your current role also nudged the prediction upward, as many people who stay tend to have longer tenure at their present organization.

Taken together, the model sees someone who is still early in their overall career, has attractive external options, and has not yet built deep roots in this specific position. These elements outweighed the stabilizing effect of your broader experience.

The company should discuss your career goals openly with you and explore whether additional responsibilities, clearer growth paths, or retention incentives could reduce the risk of losing you. You, in turn, may want to reflect on how strongly those outside opportunities appeal compared with staying and advancing internally.
